memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance. He said to his servants, "Stay here with the donkey while I and the boy go over there. We will worship and then we will come back to you." - Gen 22:4-5 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Three days Abraham walked toward Moriah - three long days with his son beside him and the command weighing on his heart. Then two remarkable statements. First, he calls what he is about to do "worship": "We will worship." And second, he says, "We will come back to you" - we, both of them.

Consider that first word: worship. Abraham understood that obeying God, even at the greatest cost, is an act of worship. Worship is not only singing and joy; sometimes it is laying our most precious things on the altar in trust. The hardest obedience can be the deepest worship.

Now consider that stunning phrase: "we will come back." Abraham fully intended to obey - yet he expresses confidence that both he and Isaac would return. How? Hebrews tells us: "Abraham reasoned that God could even raise the dead" (Heb 11:19). Abraham had concluded that even if he sacrificed Isaac, God would somehow keep His promise, even through resurrection. His faith had grown to trust God beyond what he could see or understand.

This is faith at its highest - obeying God fully while trusting Him completely, even when we cannot see how the two can be reconciled. Abraham didn't understand how it would work; he simply trusted that God would keep His word. When you face a situation where obedience and God's promises seem to collide, remember Abraham. Trust that God can make a way even where you see none.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Can you view costly obedience to God as an act of worship?
- Do you trust God to keep His promises even when you can't see how?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord, teach me that even costly obedience is worship. When obedience and Your promises seem to collide, give me faith like Abraham's, to trust that You can make a way even where I see none.
Amen.
